key_insight: Supersonic turbulent shear layers become self-similar downstream across Mach number and velocity-parameter variations, and the resulting scaling laws explain how compressibility shapes growth, asymmetry, and entrainment.
engineering_relevance: These results provide practical scaling and entrainment models for predicting mixing-layer behavior in high-speed propulsion, exhaust, and aerodynamic flow-control systems.
method: Direct numerical simulations of spatially developing supersonic turbulent shear layers.
Parametric study over convective Mach number (Mc) and velocity parameter (λ).
Derivation of self-similar forms for continuity, momentum, energy, and an approximate cross-stream velocity equation.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports collapse of normalized mean velocity and turbulence profiles in the self-similar region, constant normalized Reynolds-stress peaks, linear growth of layer thickness and momentum thickness, and good agreement between the derived cross-stream velocity and DNS.
watch_item: The proposed self-similar scalings and entrainment formula are validated within DNS cases and downstream self-similar regions, so extrapolation to non-self-similar, transitional, or experimentally noisy flows should be done cautiously.
paper_title: Numerical Study of Compressibility and Velocity Parameter Effects on Spatially Evolving Supersonic Turbulent Shear Layers
